utterances.text: Yes, I accept that. And which do you say are the crime technicians there where erroneously we put "inspector," now I see, yes, Mr. -- yeah, under there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, with that caveat, Your Honours, may I ask that this be admitted into evidence and marked?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I object. First, Your Honours, I was asked by Ms. Korner during the proofing that I showed this or similar document to the witness. And the witness made a lot of changes on the document and I provided a copy to Ms. Korner, and I don't have my copy. And neither the witness had the opportunity to look at this document and then comment about it, because he made a number of changes to that document. Therefore, I'd -- first of all, I don't know if all the changes would have been made which he made; and second, the document should be given to him perhaps to study it better in order to give his comments to the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So as I understand it your objection is not to the admission in principle. It is that it is not -- it's probably premature, that there's something that should be done --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honours. I don't object to the admission of the document because it just lists the people who were members of the CSB during the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, that's why I gave him the opportunity to look at it and he said with that exception, that they're not inspectors. We made all the changes that we could decipher, if I can put it that way, but I'm perfectly happy to have it marked for identification at this stage, give a hard copy to the witness, and tomorrow morning he can come back and tell us again if there's any further changes he thinks need making.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That's a perfectly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, so we can proceed in that manner. Yes. So the document is admitted but marked for identification -- or the document is marked for identification, sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2355 marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Having dealt with that document that you were asked about, I want to look, please, at some of the payroll lists for some of the stations that -- SJBs that came under your authority. And can we start, please, with 20190, which is in tab pre-1C [Realtime transcript read in error "31C"]. Now, this is not -- in fact, as we can see, this deals with Novo Sarajevo. And it's not a full list, but it's actually a list, according to this, of those who were omitted from the initial payroll from the month of April 1992 by a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please -- I'm sorry, could you please call the tab number, I don't --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, it's very -- it's pre-1C. It's the third document in the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Okay. It's recorded "31C."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry. Pre as in p-r-e. Sorry about the numbering.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, Novo Sarajevo, can you tell us, please, did you know these officers, first of all, Mr. Subotic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Him and Drago Jugovic both, these being the only two men I knew.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you know Mr. Slavko Aleksic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The only Slavko Aleksic I met was the one we called "The Duke." I met him during the war at Grbavica. I'm not sure if it's the same person. It doesn't say here, does it?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, can I show you, please, a photograph and see if you can recognise him. If I can find out where it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Would Your Honours forgive me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Ms. Korner, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, sorry. We'll have to leave the photograph and come back to it. Over the page, please. Or is it all on one page? It is in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So you knew Mr. Subotic, Mr. Jugovic, and those are the only two you knew. Were they members of the crime police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Mirko Subotic worked with me in the Sarajevo SUP. Drago Jugovic was with the traffic police of the Sarajevo SUP and that's why I know them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's look, please, at another document which is 20191, pre -- the tab is pre - p-r-e - 1C.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That's 1D.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, 1D. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Presumably you're familiar with these payrolls, are you not, Mr. Tusevljak, these type of payrolls?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I know the type of payrolls. But I've never seen this specific one before.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. It's a list for Ilidza, April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think we need to pull down the thing. I'm sorry about the way it was photographed. Presumably it was in a book, as you can see. Can we just highlight that. Highlight the top bit, please, zoom in, I mean. April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It shows Mr. Kovac as the chief; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we go, please, to the third page of this document, and this is April. Preferably the right way up.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: After number 81 can you read out what it says, please, if you can read it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Department for fighting crime and crime prevention.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. So is that your department that we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. When the security services centre was set up, this department belonged to the -- not the service as such but the station, because the station was part of the centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, quite. Does that show on the face of this document that it had a chief and operatives between numbers 82 to 93?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but not all of these are operatives.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the month of April 1992 those of us who had left Sarajevo stopped receiving our salaries. We no longer received our salaries from the republican secretariat of the interior of Bosnia and Herzegovina. This is a one-time financial subsidy to those police officers who had left Sarajevo. You can see that each received 25.000 dinars, the same amount for each and every one. You can see who reported in April, because they were somewhere in the area covered by the Ilidza Public Security Station, and if they were there they received the 25.000 dinars specified here. The list was drawn up for that purpose, in order to give financial support to these men. It doesn't mean that they were actually performing these activities, these jobs, at the time. Since Ilidza was a police station that remained in the hands of the Serbian MUP, the building itself, we have some operatives here who even before the war worked in that police station in addition to all these others who reported.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Of course you have to say that, don't you, because on this list of people that we see there, they all appear on the list that we looked at earlier which you said were the disappeared operatives, don't they?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Let's have up for a moment -- I don't know whether we can do it side by side, the document which is the Defence document - I'll just give the number again - it's 1D575.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, this is tab 149, but I don't see the basis to say that the witness said were the disappeared operatives?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: He says these were people that were not working during the month of April. That's what his list is about.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I must say I don't recall that, but perhaps maybe we can clarify.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think he's just said it a moment ago as well. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It's okay --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, he said it -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If you say so, I believe you now. It's --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's page 54 --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I might have missed --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yeah, okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Those are exactly the same --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, we need the second page in -- anyway, down there, we can see it -- sorry, sorry, go back to the first page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Those are the same people, aren't they, in slightly different order but the same people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but I don't see Milorad Susic; Stankic, Miri [phoen]; Ranko Sajic, I don't see them on this 15th of May list, Jamir [phoen] Dragan. So at one point they appear on the lists of the crime police and then as early as May they're gone.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, I don't follow that. Oh, you mean those people. I'm sorry, yes, I see. But on what possible basis, Mr. Tusevljak, do you say that these payments to these men do not reflect work they did throughout April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, because you'll find my name on one of these payrolls for April - I think it's the crime police one. I received my salary, too, the 25.000 dinars, and that was the only way for me to receive it, but as my entire family had fled by this time and had become refugees. There was no free bread or free potatoes or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So you're saying out of the kindness of its heart the MUP paid all these people something to compensate them for April even though they weren't working?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, for the most part all those who reported to the MUP got this amount.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I see the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, we have another five minutes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right, then I'll show you one more document. Could you have a look, please, at 2192, please, the payroll list for Sokolac.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We can take off the other one. Second page.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovcanin; Predrag Cajic; Mr. Cobovic, Veljko; were they all part of the crime investigation department?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they probably were, in Sokolac.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you would say, would you, that these payrolls are not evidence that any of these people worked at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This only proves that they received the salary. These are employees of the Sokolac Police Station who had been employees in the crime service before the war. They never left their station.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So at least in Sokolac they were operating throughout, were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were operating then or not -- I wasn't in Sokolac in April. I didn't go to Sokolac until August perhaps, so I don't know whether they were operating or not operating. I was in Nedzarici at the time. This was in April. I can't say with certainty that they were operating or that they were not operating.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, you see, it may be that I misunderstood the tenor of your evidence, Mr. Tusevljak, in which case I'll stop taking you through this rather tedious exercise of having a look at payrolls. You're not saying, are you, therefore, that no crime police were operating anywhere in Serb-held territories in the Sarajevo area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. If you understand what I mean, if I understood the question correctly, some stations functioned and in some police stations it didn't function at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you don't know one way or the other, do you, which police stations it was functioning in and which it wasn't?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, if you show me the list, I can tell you where operatives existed and where there were no operatives at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Well, have a look, please, at one last one which is -- it's 212 -- 65 ter number is -- sorry, 02127. I'm not sure why.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mrs. Korner, the previous, one you're not tendering that one?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, sorry, Your Honour, I meant to tender it. Yes, please. I forgot.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, first of all I don't know what was the nexus between the -- this witness and the document, the second -- the document is a fresh evidence, so I believe that that requires, according to the ruling of Your Honours, the Office of the Prosecution to establish certain facts. And I believe the witness said he never saw the document before.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, my understanding -- first of all, can I say that of course he says he didn't -- and I accept that, that he probably didn't see the documents before, but he says he knows these people who are members of the crime -- shown as members of the crime police, and the reason that I'm putting them in now and seeking to tender them is to go to the credibility of his assertions, which I understood to be the case, certainly, that the -- that the assembled might of the CSB Sarajevo through its component SJBs did not have members of the crime police working in the early months of the conflict. And I'll check, but I have a feeling that this document, the one for Sokolac and indeed the one for Ilidza, which I should have asked for as well, but I was just moving through a whole series, are relatively new ones. I'll just check on when we acquired them. Your Honours, could we do that -- I see what the time is now. Could we just do that over the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. Before we rise, I -- I'm advised it is necessary to issue a formal order lifting the confidentiality of the transcript from pages 6 -- from page 6, line 13, onwards, which I now do. So we take the break now and resume at -- in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: While the witness is on his way back in, I am reminded by the Court Officer that in terms of the order that was made just before we took the break about lifting the confidentiality, that it should be made clear that that also extends to the audio files.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, yes. I'm sorry. Your Honours, may I also, before he comes in -- well, firstly we need to return to a ruling on the objection raised by Mr. Zecevic. Secondly, could I ask that there's ten - well, I say ten minutes because I think it may take that - to raise something that needs discussion as a result of something that was said this morning. So I will finish cross-examination, if not tomorrow, very early - touch wood - very early on Thursday morning, as I indicated before. Your Honours, so our application is these documents, and indeed I'm going to be showing some more to the witness, should be admitted on the basis that they are relevant to the assertions he's made about the operation of the crime police, and they go to his credibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if all these documents go for the credibility of the witness and not for the truth of its contents, we don't have the objection.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, that's the difficulty. Of course it goes to the truth of the contents. We say these payrolls are records -- that they don't make much sense otherwise, are records of payments made for work done and therefore contradict what he says or appears to be saying about the existence of crime police during those early months. So it's not really a truth of the contents, it's whether it advances our case. Truth of the contents is different --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, I follow you, Ms. Korner. Mr. Zecevic, the distinction which you now make, in other contexts that makes -- is easily recognisable, but having regard to these -- the nature of these documents, the "truth" is presumed, but the limited purpose for which the Prosecution is using them is in terms of credibility. So I don't think we need to concern ourselves with that distinction here, if you follow me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, but the ruling of Your Honours is that this is a fresh evidence. This obviously then is a fresh evidence which the Office of the Prosecutor is trying to introduce. That is what Ms. Korner says just right now, we are advancing our case. Now, if that is a fresh evidence, then according to the ruling and the existing jurisprudence the Office of the Prosecutor has a certain threshold to meet before these documents can be admitted. That is simply -- this is the decision of this Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, I'm reminded about that, Mr. Zecevic, but I'm wondering whether if it were only the question of credibility, this wouldn't present a problem. But I'm wondering whether the -- because the -- allowing their use to test credibility is only possible on the assumption that these are accurate and truthful records makes it necessary to invoke the ruling to which you -- to which you have referred. That's my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But, Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Or am I being overly subtle or overly complicated?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, perhaps it's my wrong understanding, Your Honours. If the -- perhaps I can explain how I understand. If the document is introduced for the credibility of the witness, that means that the Office of the Prosecutor would not rely on that document in their submissions, they will only say: This witness so and so was not telling the truth because this document was presented to him, this document was presented to him, and so on and so forth, so you cannot rely on the credibility of the witness's testimony. That is my understanding. Now, if, however, this will be the basis for Office of the Prosecutor to submit that there has been -- unlike the testimony of the witnesses and unlike other documents which we presented, that there has been a sufficient number of police officers based on these documents, then it is definitely fresh evidence. And if they wanted to establish that, they could have established that in the -- during the case of the Prosecution. Therefore, that is my understanding and that is why I think the Office of the Prosecutor needs to meet threshold to be -- to have these documents admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I fully understand what you're saying, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I think there's a missing link, as it were, in what Mr. Zecevic is saying. Firstly, you could only challenge the credibility of a witness using a document which you believed to be true, because you should not be challenging the credibility of a witness on a document you did not rely on the contents of. Secondly, a number of these documents had been used by the Defence themselves. Thirdly, it's no good saying "we didn't prove this as part of our case." We asserted throughout that there were effectively sufficient people to do the investigations because they were doing other investigations, and it's only when a witness comes along and says - which cannot be anticipated - in terms -- not just the general "everything was chaotic," but that "we did not have sufficient manpower to carry out investigations," that we're entitled to challenge that assertion through these documents. And obviously to that extent it bolsters our case. But we don't know what these Defence witnesses are going to say. So that's the situation, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The Chamber's of the view that the relevance of this material only becomes patent because of the witness's testimony. And as Ms. Korner has correctly pointed out, the Prosecution would not have been in a position to anticipate this; and therefore, in the circumstances, we agree that it could be admitted and marked, and we so order.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then, Your Honours, could I ask, please, that the documents which have a 65 ter number 2010 -- sorry, I say that again, 20191 and 20192 be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I -- of course I object, and I strongly suggest that the ruling that you just made is -- departs from the previous oral ruling of this Trial Chamber. Because if it's the fresh evidence, Your Honours, there are other options for the Office of the Prosecutor. They can ask for rebuttal, they can ask for a re-opening of their case, but the fresh evidence it must be treated in accordance with the jurisprudence, and that was the decision of this Trial Chamber. Now we are having a different situation. And I'm afraid I would -- we would have to consult, but I might be -- I might be asking for a certificate on this matter, Your Honours. This is a very important matter for the presentation of the Defence case. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I just say one word about this. It's not fresh evidence. It's evidence that we've been using, both sides, throughout the course of the case, these payrolls, for different aspects. Therefore, if a witness comes along and says - as this witness has - the crime police during the early months were not in existence and therefore couldn't operate, it must be right that documents which are used to challenge that assertion should be placed into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner, we've gone over this ground and raked and re-raked it. And no doubt we would be invited to re-visit it again. But for the time being the last application you made in terms of the -- of those documents mentioned at lines -- page 64, lines 11 and 12, we make the like order.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, therefore document 20191 shall be Exhibit P2356 and document 20192 shall be Exhibit P2357. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Tusevljak, I just want to be sure I understand this. Is it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: 20190 was not tendered?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I'm coming back to that. I was dealing with that for a different purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Tusevljak, do I understand you to say that it is your case that the payments that we see all over these documents for April are simply, if you understand the expression, ex gratia payments made by the MUP to help out Serbian police officers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mainly, yes. That was the first time that we received the 25.000 dinars. That was in May. We hadn't received any salary in February or in March in the police in Sarajevo, which was a part of the Republic of B&H.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: However, that is not your contention, I take it, for salaries paid in May; in other words, in May if a salary was paid, that was to people who had actually worked in May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that the salary for May was the same for everybody, both the active and the reserve police staff. It was the same. I think there was no difference in the amount of the salaries. That's my opinion. I can't really go into that because I didn't make the decision on the payrolls and I didn't make a decision on who was not to be paid. That was not my job. I don't know what else I can say about this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, no, I think you misunderstood, or it's possible it's a translation difficulty. Regardless of what they got paid, people who were paid in May or for work done in May, that was for actual work performed. It was not an ex gratia payment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I really can't comment on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Tusevljak, you're the one who's been making these assertions about nobody being able to work, so I want to show you some payrolls for May if I may now. Let's see if you can help on those. First of all, can you look at the payroll which is 20195 at tab 2D, although it's a slightly different point here that I want to make. Now, do you agree that appears to be a payroll for May for Kula?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So there was a distinction made between Kula and Novo Sarajevo station, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And are the people who are being paid here criminal inspectors, four of them I think, plus an analyst?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, at that moment, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And do you know those people there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So in May of 1992, Kula had an operating criminal investigation department?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the police station with these people, yes. They all should have been working, but I think Rajko Gluhovic never worked either in Kula or in Novo Sarajevo, and I think Mirko Ljuboje wasn't working at all then either because he was at the police station in Vojkovici.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. But -- wherever they were based at the time. And according to this they were paid different salaries?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This was based on level of education. It was university education, secondary education, or post-secondary education. It didn't go based on position but based on the level of education.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And do you recognise the signature? It says "nacelnik," and there's a signature -- "chief," sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I ask that this document be exhibited for two reasons. The first is - and I'm not clear that it was actually an assertion made by the witness, it's right to say, but certainly Mr. Zecevic - that Kula didn't exist and there was Novo Sarajevo. And secondly, the assertion as to crime police working.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I object. I don't want to explain the assertions of the witness. The witness gave his testimony. This document was never disclosed to the Defence. Now -- before, I mean, it was announced for this witness. So as I said before, this is -- this, in our opinion, is intolerable that during the Defence case the Office of the Prosecutor is allowed to lead evidence and advance their case like they're in the -- during their OTP case. Therefore, I strongly object.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm told - and it may be -- - that this was disclosed in 2009 in batch 78 under the number 0665-2364 through to -2666. And we've given it ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: What is the document we're talking about right now?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's the one on the screen, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yeah, and the tab number, is that --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, the tab is 2D.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Still 2D. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, that's one of the two documents we admitted a few moments ago; right?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: No?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So, Your Honour, this is a Kula document. You admitted earlier the documents in relation to the other police stations. This is Kula for May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Sorry, it's 2D. Sorry about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's quite all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But, Mr. Zecevic, there is obviously a difference in opinion as to whether this is or is not fresh evidence. But I would have thought that according to Rule 90(H), I think it is, the cross-examining party is required to put its case to the witness, in any case. So I wonder whether this is really as you say, to be classified as new evidence, so fresh evidence, in the sense that you seem to use this phrase.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may, according to the jurisprudence of this Tribunal, the fresh evidence are: Material that was not included on the OTP's 65 ter list, material not admitted during OTP case in chief, material tendered by the OTP when cross-examining the Defence witness. So, in my opinion, this definitely -- each of these documents qualify hundred per cent as a fresh evidence, and that is our position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not disputing the 90(H), of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: No, but obviously the implications of what you have just read out to me is that the Prosecution or the cross-examining party would be barred from providing any new witness -- any new evidence, and that is clearly not the intention of the Rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, with all due respect, the -- I'm not saying they should be banned all together, but this is exceptional circumstances when they can -- when they can introduce the fresh evidence. That is -- that is the nature of the jurisprudence in this Tribunal. Otherwise, Your Honours, we prepared the Defence case based on the case to answer. If that case changes, like it changes in this situation, how are we supposed to give our defence to that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: But in any event, Mr. Zecevic, returning to the document at issue now, whereas we fully understand your position on these documents generally, now that the matter of disclosure is out of the way, because I confess that that would have caused me some concern had it not been previously disclosed, this is assimilated to the position of the earlier documents we admitted, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I still don't have the confirmation from my assistants about the disclosure of these documents. What I have as a note is that the document was never disclosed to us before. Perhaps it might be the -- we -- Your Honours, it will take us some time because it might be a different ERN number, because that is the only way how we can check the documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what kind of search engine or the facilities the Office of the Prosecutor has, but we don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, can I ask, for the moment, until the Defence have had a chance to confirm it, that it be marked for identification so that we can move on and perhaps return to this tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Or at the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we'd so mark it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I'll repeat again: The number under which it was disclosed was 06665-2364 [sic] in a range that goes up to 2666, and it was in 2009, batch 78. So I hope that assists.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, therefore 65 ter number 20195 shall become P2358 marked for identification. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. On the same topic, and then we'll move on to something different, could you have a look, please, at 20198 at tab 2G. This is apparently a payroll for May for Vogosca. And if we look at the first page, at numbers 26, 27, and 29 -- it's a bit I think -- yes. Thank you very much. Does that show them as members of the criminal investigation department?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you have a closer look, 26, 27, 29, you will see that they are crossed out. It's crossed out. It says: Paid according to the payroll of national security. 26, he left, so he wasn't paid at all. And then 29, Slobodan Govedarica, paid according to the payroll of the Pale SJB.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Meaning no one, none of these persons from the Vogosca Police Station, in May received a salary, and this document demonstrates that in no uncertain terms if you look closely.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you look closely.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It shows they were paid by other places; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. It shows they were not on the payroll of the Vogosca Public Security Station. Zivko Lazarevic now works for the national security. Stanko Borovcanin, also crossed out, he used to be chief up until April 1992 for that same police station, but it reads here he left. He's no longer there. Slobodan Govedarica was paid by the Pale SJB. Therefore, as I said, there are no crime police in Vogosca.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you go over the page, please, to number 35. Nebojsa Lazic, criminal inspector, 50.000, signed for.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nebojsa Lazic. I never heard of anyone like that working at the Vogosca Police Station.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, it appears, according to you, this is an accurate payroll because these people, who you knew, who -- went elsewhere. All you can say about this gentleman is you've never heard of him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, never.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can we look, then, please, at one different one, then. Could you look, please, at 20197, tab 2F. This is Rogatica for May. And we need to go, I think, to the second page at numbers 36 and 37 and -- well, 36 and 37, inspectors, and at 38 a criminal technician. Did you know Mr. - I think it's Zoranovic - and Mr. Perkovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But do you agree it would appear that Rogatica in May had at least two people or three people working in its criminal investigations department?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think this is again a payroll. I think Rogatica at the time was still not in the hands of the VRS. There was fighting going on there throughout. I really don't know. I don't know these people from this period, and I said that Rogatica was not under the Sarajevo SUP. Their heads and the chiefs were people I didn't know back then. I did meet some of them in the latter half of 1992 when we started organising meetings.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, whether you knew it or not - and I'm not quite clear what the fact is that Rogatica was still being fought over has to do with this - I'm suggesting to you that if one looked at the payrolls for all of these SJBs that one would find that they had people working in the criminal investigation departments in May. Do you understand that? Do you understand, Mr. Tusevljak, that is the suggestion that I make to you, that you are wrong when you say there was no criminal investigation department during this early period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I'm not saying that these people weren't inspectors, but as for that department dealing with crime-related business at this point in time indicated here, I'm certain that that was not the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can we move then, please, to the general topic of communications. Now, again I want to make sure that we understand what you're saying. Are you saying that during the period up until July of 1992 the CSB Sarajevo was not communicating with any of the SJBs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that's not what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well just can you tell us, please, shortly, what you are saying about communications with the SJBs within your area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I never worked in the communications department or had anything to do with communications at all. What I do know is that there were problems when I came to the security services centre. The dispatches that were sent to the subsidiary stations from the centre were late. The same thing applied to the reports. As for everything else, the method of communication that was used by the communications centre, what equipment was used, what technology was used, is something that I can't tell you about because I understand nothing about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No -- yes, I understand that, and I'm not asking you about the technical equipment. What I'm asking you is -- and I'm asking you, for example, because of something you said at page 22241. You were asked: "The CSB Sarajevo Romanija-Birac, did it have any communication with the public security station of Ilidza?" And you said: "No. There was that communication that I drew for you," in other words, it was put to you that if someone from the CSB traverses 160 kilometres to get to Ilidza. So are you saying there was no communication except by dispatch -- by courier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: More often than not it was by courier. We did consider a document which showed that at one point in time a telefax line was being used and it was down to Ilidza to use their courier service to forward the dispatches to the stations in their area, Pale to the stations in their own area, and then Sokolac and Zvornik and whatever else. I can't quite remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, yes, all right. That's fair enough. Can I say, I'm not suggesting that in many areas communication was not difficult during this period. But it is not right to say, is it, that there was no communication, in other words, orders going from the CSB and reports being received from the SJB -- sorry, I'll start that sentence again. It got a bit lost. Sorry. You're not suggesting, are you, that the CSB could not send orders or dispatches to any of the SJBs under its authority during the period April until July?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, the dispatches that we sent or received were forwarded in a variety of ways to the police station by courier or whatever else, but we always had situations where the dispatches were late.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Look, this is a simple question. As I say, I accept that there may well have been problems and things were late or even went missing, but it is not the case, is it, that the CSB was unable to send its dispatches or orders to any police station, any SJB?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, if we wrote them, we sent them. But I don't know how.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Equally, it was possible, wasn't it, for each of the SJBs within the area of responsibility of the CSB Sarajevo to send its reports to the CSB?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First of all, you must know that in April there is no established centre. In May, you still don't have an established centre. The centre first began to get off the ground sometime in June. Therefore, there was no address that the police stations could use to send their reports to, as far as the security services centre was concerned.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. I'm going to ask you to have a look, please, at the communications log-book of the Ministry of the Interior, which is Exhibit 1428, tab 1A. Now, are you familiar with this book, Mr. Tusevljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I've never seen it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, to begin with, is this right, the MUP headquarters and the CSB Sarajevo shared the same premises in the Vrace school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were there in the Vrace school but not with these guys. I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, which guys?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The school at Vrace had several buildings. If you look at where the minister was and his services, it was in the same place where the centre chief was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I see. All right. It was -- I see what you mean. So it was a different building within the complex that made up Vrace; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. You may not be familiar with the earlier entries which is -- which deal with a -- the dispatches or the documents sent out by MUP headquarters to the various places and received, but I want you to have a look, please, at item number 74 - but it turned into the Sarajevo book at some stage, apparently - at -- it's, in English, at the fifth page. Let's just check if it is in the -- in B/C/S it is -- it's quite difficult to tell, I'm afraid. It's got at the top 0339-2402, if that helps.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the -- at page 75, line 24, the answer is: "Yes." And then the sentence beginning: "You may not be familiar ..." is the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Is that a dispatch from the SJB Milici reporting on those killed, missing, and mutilated in the Birac area sent apparently on the 16th of July to be received by you, Mr. Tusevljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't see a date here. It was sent to me, that much is certain, but I can't see a date. It was probably sometime in July.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't really see the date. It says Milici Public Security Station, report on --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yeah, it appears -- well, you're right. And I'm not quite sure where the date comes from, but certainly the date is on the following entry of the 15th of July. So we can see the previous -- it's somewhere between the 14th and the 15th because at number 72, if we go back one page, we'll see the date there. Did you get a dispatch from the Milici SJB reporting on people killed in Birac, missing and et cetera?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably. That's what it says. And my signature should be somewhere there too.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, we can't see a signature, unless that's your signature above there. And just for these purposes can we look at a few more entries that appear to be for you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: At number -- well, probably 107, please, which we'll find in the B/C/S at page 3, 0339-2407. And the English at page 10.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Is that the instruction that was sent to the SJBs of the meeting that you had with the crime heads in Sokolac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I see here that 107 is dispatch to call a meeting for Sokolac. It was a dispatch that was sent out in order for a meeting to be called.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, doesn't it read at 107: "Scheduling of meeting of the CJB crime department and CSB in Sokolac"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, a meeting that we had.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And the book contains a large number of entries, which I don't want to take you through because it's going to take a long time, that relate to investigations into the Tas factory thefts in Vogosca. Would you agree that that took up, certainly in 1992, a great deal of your time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Based on the requests that we received from the RS Assembly and MUP. And you see that there were no crime police at all in Vogosca. So I only have these two operatives and I couldn't expect them to do ten jobs at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. The question was: Do you agree it took -- the investigations into the thefts at the Tas factory took up a lot of your time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course. The crime police took some time to investigate that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We'll come back to that later. So certainly by July no -- would you agree, absolutely no problem in communications with anybody?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By July?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: By July.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, you see that I only received the first dispatch on the 15th of July.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What about my communications? Where are my dispatches?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, you -- you can go through all of the book if you want to, Mr. Tusevljak, but are you suggesting that even in July you couldn't communicate with your SJBs -- your crime police in the SJBs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I'm saying is there were ongoing difficulties with the communications. The communication lines were not working properly as they would have in normal circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, still on the subject of communications, and I'm going to show you some other documents probably tomorrow now, you drew this map when you were interviewed in Sarajevo and you were asked to draw further maps by Mr. Zecevic or to mark further maps, I should say accurately. I want to see, because it's quite difficult to see the perspective in some of those maps, whether you agree with this one. Could you have a look, please -- what was the -- it's 65 ter 20207, tab 42A? Now, the difficulty about the maps that you were looking at is it didn't show places like Pale and whatever. What we have attempted to do here - and have a look at it and see if you agree, and if necessary you can take the map away with you overnight in hard copy - is indicate by the red line that goes down the left of the page there the front line. To the left being -- of that red line being the ABiH or Croat-held areas; to the right, the Serb areas. And then you'll see we've indicated the other areas which were part of the front lines. Have a look at that and see whether you agree with that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know which period this was in.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It changed the most in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I'm suggesting that this is --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. When I'm looking at this now, it turns out that all of Hadzici was under the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. It's meant to indicate that part of Hadzici was part of the Serbian republic, do you see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not this small an area.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's the same situation with Trnovo. I'm not sure about that part of Rogatica because I was never there, and I'm not sure about that part of Srebrenica, Bratunac, Vlasenica because I wasn't there either. And I'm not sure about the area towards Kladanj, Olovo, Vares, Breza, Visoko, Kiseljak because I was never there either.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. What I'm trying to indicate - and let's see if we can get at it this way, rather tediously - is that from where you were based in the Lukavica barracks -- or, not barracks, next to -- in the electro -- or next to the Lukavica barracks, you could travel to Pale, to Sokolac, to Han Pijesak, and further up without any difficulty?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, except to Pale because you had to cross Trebevic and that was difficult because of combat operations. So you had to travel down the macadam road that I described.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. But otherwise, as it were, you had, I suppose, to use an expression that we've heard over and over again, a corridor through which you could travel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, thank you. That's all I wanted to get at. And as far as the snipers are concerned, any Muslim snipers that there were, were based in, as it were, Sarajevo itself, weren't they, the town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Sarajevo and also where Ilidza bordered on the other side, from the line of Mount Igman, there was constant sniper fire on Kotorac Donji, Kotorac Gornji, that part of Butmir, Novakovice, Kuce. This wasn't towards the inner area of Sarajevo but the outside, and the situation was same towards Visoko, Breza, and so on. There was snipers that were shooting from Sarajevo. And it wasn't just snipers, it was also Brownings and other weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, but you were up in the hills, weren't you, whereas the snipers were down in the valley of Sarajevo, the Muslim-held areas of Sarajevo? Leaving aside Igman. Leaving aside Igman. But from where you were.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's not correct, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Where do you say the Muslim snipers were in connection to where you were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wasn't on the Muslim side, but I know where the Serbian victims were. And since I know the town of Sarajevo very well, just as I said about the areas where I'd never been, I don't know them. At the separation line in Grbavica, which goes along the Miljacka River, on the one side there are 12- and 13-storey residential buildings as are on the other side. Further on, Gola Brda is a place that was under the control of the BH army the whole time, and from that position they targeted the Vrace-Lukavica road. Mojmilo hill is another position that was under the control of the BH army the whole time and they constantly targeted the Lukavica-Kula road or the positions or Serbian villages in Nedzarici.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Also, if you go towards Vogosca, this position or this recurrent theme that the Serbs were on the hills and somebody was defending themselves from the city is simply not true. In our official report which we filed - and I'm not going to name names now - but we filed it against responsible people, people who were responsible for the sniper activity from Sarajevo, if you ever get the opportunity, I have that official report and I can show it to you, and you'll see the victims of these snipers on this side. This entire case file is with the Bosnian prosecutor's office --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Stop. I'm sorry, Mr. Tusevljak, for a number of reasons. Firstly, we need some time to discuss. But secondly, the only point that I'm raising with you - and I can see you disagree with me - is that when you allege that you could not travel to these places because of snipers, that that cannot be right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it's not correct. Our roads ran across Mount Trebevic, and the defence line with the Serbian army was under this road, was 2 metres under this road. This means that the defence line ran along that road. And travelling down that road was always a matter of life and death.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. We'll leave it there, thank you very much, for today.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may, I'd like to raise just one matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Tusevljak, again we have certainly procedural matters to deal with before we rise for the day, so the usher will escort you out before we rise. And we will resume your cross-examination tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I ask that he be handed the CSB chart that Mr. Zecevic wants him to look at which was MFI'd.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, what I -- what I wanted to raise is the question of intercepts and their probative value. Today I was the one taken by surprise when Mr. Zecevic said that there was no evidence before the Court that the people on the transcripts, in this case Mr. Tintor and Mr. Veselinovic, actually had that conversation. My understanding of the admission of those intercepts was that it was accepted, through the evidence of the witness that dealt with them, that the people named are the people who spoke. And we were in fact prevented from taking it any further on that basis; that if they were admitted, they were admitted. Now, Your Honours, I would really like to know that my understanding is correct, because otherwise we've just got a series of meaningless pieces of paper in evidence, if the Defence supposition or suggestion that was made by Mr. Zecevic is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I would have thought, though, Ms. Korner, and it has been a while since we had to deal with this, that the Chamber's view would have been made patent at the time that we admitted these transcripts, and therefore the -- I would have thought that the first step in your present concerns would be to see what we said at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, that was my understanding, Your Honours, from what you said at the time. And it's apparently not Mr. Zecevic's understanding, but then -- so I'm seeking clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, I suppose, if -- the Chamber will have to look at the transcript and any ruling we would have made, and if clarification is necessary, we would then address it. But as I said, for myself, I thought this matter was settled at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, so did I until this came up again today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, do you have any reply to this?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Your Honour, we understand this to be two separate issues. One issue is the admittance of the intercept, and they are admitted; the second issue is the probative value of each of the intercepts and the weight to be given to the intercepts, which depends on many factors, including proof of authenticity, namely, whether there is a proof of the identity of the speaker. Certain intercepts, for example, have been played to the witness and they recognise the speakers; some others have never been played. For example, if I can give you one example. Concerning the intercept that Ms. Korner was showing to the witness, the witness says in his statement, and based on that statement this intercept was admitted, he said: I listened to the tape of one telephone conversation --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think we ought to be in private session, Your Honours. The witness testified in --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, I'm not going to mention the witness or anything. I'm just reading what he -- what he said. It says --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Out of an abundance of caution, we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
